subject: Mathematics
title: Cartesian Products & Ordered Pairs
quickSummary: An Ordered Pair (a, b) obeys coordinate order. Kuratowski defined (a, b) = {{a}, {a, b}}. The Cartesian product A × B has cardinality |A| · |B|.
summary: Master ordered pairs, Kuratowski axiomatic set construction, Cartesian products A × B, R^2 and R^3 spaces, and algebraic product identities.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1. Formal Definition of Ordered Pairs & Kuratowski Set Construction
conceptBreakdown.title: 1. Formal Definition of Ordered Pairs & Kuratowski Set Construction

summaryBox.title: Axiomatic Core
summaryBox.takeaway: (a, b) = (c, d) ⟺ a = c and b = d. Set-theoretically defined by Kuratowski as (a, b) ≡ {{a}, {a, b}}.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
KURATOWSKI SET CONSTRUCTION
                   
   Ordered Pair (a, b)  ──►  Outer Set {{a}, {a, b}}
                                ├── Singleton {a}     ──► Identifies 1st Element 'a'
                                └── Unordered Pair {a, b} ──► Identifies 2nd Element 'b'
conceptBreakdown.content:
An **Ordered Pair** $(a, b)$ is a pair of objects where the order of appearance is significant. Unlike an unordered set $\{a, b\}$ where $\{a, b\} = \{b, a\}$, an ordered pair obeys:

$$\mathbf{(a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c \quad \text{and} \quad b = d}$$

### Axiomatic Definition (Kuratowski, 1921)
To ground ordered pairs purely within set theory, Kazimierz Kuratowski defined the ordered pair as a set of sets:
$$\mathbf{(a, b) \equiv \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\}}$$

*Proof of Uniqueness*: If $\{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} = \{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\}$, comparing singleton elements forces $\{a\} = \{c\} \implies a = c$. Then $\{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} = \{\{a\}, \{a, d\}\} \implies b = d$. $\blacksquare$

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.2 The Cartesian Product A × B and Higher Dimensions
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.2 The Cartesian Product A × B and Higher Dimensions
conceptBreakdown.content:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two non-empty sets. The **Cartesian Product** $A \times B$ is the set of all ordered pairs $(a, b)$ such that $a \in A$ and $b \in B$:
$$\mathbf{A \times B = \{(a, b) \mid a \in A \land b \in B\}}$$

- **Cardinality Rule**: If $|A| = m$ and $|B| = n$, then $\mathbf{|A \times B| = |A| \cdot |B| = m \cdot n}$.
- **Empty Set Product**: If either $A = \emptyset$ or $B = \emptyset$, then $A \times B = \emptyset$.
- **Real Plane ($\mathbb{R}^2 = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$)**: $\mathbb{R}^2 = \{(x, y) \mid x \in \mathbb{R}, y \in \mathbb{R}\}$. Geometrically represents the 2D Cartesian plane.
- **Real 3-Space ($\mathbb{R}^3 = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$)**: $\mathbb{R}^3 = \{(x, y, z) \mid x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}\}$. Geometrically represents 3D Euclidean space.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.3 Algebraic Identities of Cartesian Products
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.3 Algebraic Identities of Cartesian Products
conceptBreakdown.content:
| Property / Identity | Mathematical Formulation |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Non-Commutativity** | $A \times B \neq B \times A$ (unless $A = B$ or $A = \emptyset$ or $B = \emptyset$) |
| **Distributivity over Union** | $A \times (B \cup C) = (A \times B) \cup (A \times C)$ |
| **Distributivity over Intersection** | $A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)$ |
| **Distributivity over Difference** | $A \times (B \setminus C) = (A \times B) \setminus (A \times C)$ |
| **Intersection of Products** | $\mathbf{(A \times B) \cap (C \times D) = (A \cap C) \times (B \cap D)}$ |
| **Complement Identity** | $(A \times B)' = (A' \times B') \cup (A' \times B) \cup (A \times B')$ |
